## Prune acknowledgements that excuse nothing, fired on Nucleation

*2026-11-04 00:25:45*

`luria repair --prune_stale` (`luria/prune.py`, [ADR-138](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-138.md), [#385](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/385)) removes
acknowledgement codes that answer for no site, and deletes a directive left
naming nothing.

**Fired on a real case before trusting it.** This ran on a scratch worktree
of Nucleation at the head of [dmarx/nucleation#391](https://github.com/dmarx/nucleation/pull/391), after that PR had
removed its 69 wholly unused directives by hand. It found 336 idle codes in
262 files, all in directives that were otherwise in use, and none of them
whole directives. That matches a count taken independently, from
`Citation.excused_by`, before the module existed. The guard's re-scan found
the loud citations unchanged, `stale_annotations()` was 0 before and after,
and a second run found nothing. The sampled diffs removed only the idle
code and left the reason text as it was.

**The guard was fired on a sabotaged prune**
(`test_the_guard_restores_the_files_when_a_finding_changes`). `_idle` is
patched to call every code idle, so a directive that is answering for a
citation gets removed. The re-scan sees the citation go loud, restores the
file, and raises with the code named.

**Traps.**

- `used(ann)` is per directive. A per-code question has to go through
  `excused_by`, and that is matched by identity (`id(ann)`), since
  `Annotation` is a frozen dataclass whose equal copies would collide.
- Findings are compared by (file, code) count, not by line. Deleting a
  directive line moves every citation under it, so a by-line comparison
  fails on every whole-directive removal.
- `mention-ok` cannot use `excused_by`. The acknowledgement program gives a
  site to the first state-claiming directive and to a `mention-ok` only
  failing that. A mention whose site an `inactive-ok` holds today looks
  idle, and deleting it would lose the cover [ADR-105](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-105.md) wants when the document
  goes Active.
- A first draft found the cited codes per directive by scanning every site.
  That is quadratic: six thousand directives against the whole record's
  sites. The sites are indexed by file first.

## unconcretize, fired on nucleation#387

*2026-11-04 04:47:32*

`luria unconcretize CODE...` (`luria/unconcretize.py`, [ADR-140](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-140.md)) gives a
numbered document its number back as a temporary code.

**Fired on the real case before trusting it.** The case was nucleation#387,
whose branch filed `ADR-068` while the trunk merged a different `ADR-068`. In a
scratch worktree of that branch:

- `unconcretize ADR-068` renamed it `ADR-tmpuzsbf` in about 3 seconds and
  rewrote three files: the document's heading, `luria.yaml` (five comments
  and blurbs) and a changelog fragment, whose link label and target both
  changed.
- After a commit, `git merge origin/main` was clean. The add/add conflict
  was gone.
- `concretize` then numbered the document `ADR-069`, recorded `formerly:
  ADR-tmpuzsbf`, and rewrote all five `luria.yaml` citations.

**Traps.**

- **`concretize` never rewrote `luria.yaml`.** A temporary code cited in a
  config comment survived concretization as a dangling code. The fix is
  one file list, `concretize.rewritable_files`, which both commands read,
  config included. The fired case found it: before the change, `ADR-069`'s
  five config citations would have stayed `ADR-tmpuzsbf`.
- **Plain replacement is safe for a temporary tail and wrong for a
  number.** `LIT-156` is a prefix of `LIT-1563`, and nucleation has
  four-digit codes. The match is whole-token, and excludes a preceding `-`,
  so `LU-ADR-068` is not touched.
- **Giving back several numbers in one commit ties them** for concretize's
  commit-time order. The renumbering test asserts contiguity and survival,
  not which document takes which number.
- **The first design scoped the rewrite to lines added since a merge
  base.** It refused mid-merge, and refused documents that predate the
  branch. The owner rejected it: the user names the document, and the
  command should not be relative to a commit. Running before the merge
  gives the collision fix without it.

## A scratch HOME hides user site-packages from a subprocess test

*2026-11-26 00:24:03*

`tests/test_encoding.py` runs `luria init`, `index` and `lint` in a subprocess
under an ASCII locale, with `HOME` set to the test's tmp_path so nothing
leaks in. In an environment where luria's dependencies were installed into
the user site-packages (root's `~/.local` here), that scratch `HOME` hides
them: the subprocess died on `import jinja2`, and both behavioural tests
reported "init crashed under an ASCII locale" — an import error dressed as
the encoding failure the tests exist to catch. CI's runner installs into the
system site-packages, so it never showed there.

Fix: one `ascii_env()` helper for both tests, passing the parent's
`sys.path` as `PYTHONPATH`. The import path has nothing to do with the
encoding under test.

Fired before trusting ([DP-006](../../record/principles.d/DP-006.md)): with `writes.py` switched to
`encoding="ascii"`, the behavioural test fails on `UnicodeEncodeError … '—'`
— the real failure — and passes again once restored.

The trap generalizes: any subprocess test that scrubs `HOME` for isolation
also scrubs the user site. Pass the import path explicitly.

## Measuring the Quartz site build from CI history, and a weekly timed build

*2026-11-26 18:52:39*

**The question.** Published records were getting slow to build and heavy to
open, and the plan is to replace Quartz. The requirements had to come from
what CI had already recorded, not from a local benchmark. So the data is
every `pages.yml` run of luria (365 runs), nucleation (584) and
mathematics-of-meaning (157), with per-step durations for samples of 32, 26
and 1 build jobs, and 23 build logs. The numbers are in [ADR-148](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-148.md)'s
context. In one line: luria holds flat at about 90 s; nucleation's site step
went from 61 s (2026-09-25) to 2731 s (2026-11-25), near-linear in its
artifact (r = 0.985, n = 18); Quartz's emit phase is 84% of the build.

**Traps in the CI data, for whoever reads it next.**

- *Run duration is not build time* in nucleation. A gate job and the `pages`
  concurrency group can hold a run queued: one run reads 2814 s and skipped
  its build. 75 "successful" runs of 60 s or less are gate no-ops. Use the
  build job's own `started_at`/`completed_at`.
- *Logs are tailed to 5,000 lines* by the API, and since 2026-10-03
  nucleation's tail is entirely `upload-pages-artifact`'s tar listing (about
  49k lines on 2026-11-25). Quartz's phase lines were readable for only five
  nucleation builds. This is why the timed build keeps its own Quartz log in
  an artifact and writes only phase lines to the job log.
- *Artifacts are kept for a day* and logs older than about three months
  return 410, so the history can't be re-read later. The weekly `site-perf`
  artifact is kept for 90 days.
- *Quartz rounds its own totals* with `pretty-time`: a 40-minute build reads
  "40m", a 58-second phase "58s". `luria.site_perf stamp` adds
  sub-millisecond stamps to every line.
- *luria's September outliers* (site step 506 s and 631 s on 2026-09-03) were
  Quartz 4.5.2's npm install taking 4–5 minutes, not the build. Quartz 5
  installs in 5–6 s.

**Found along the way.** mathematics-of-meaning has never published: all 157
runs fail in `luria site` with `yaml.scanner.ScannerError: mapping values are
not allowed in this context` while parsing a document's frontmatter, under
luria 0.35.0 and 1.10.x alike. That is a bug in the record, the reader, or
both, independent of Quartz, and should be fixed on its own. Separately, at
nucleation's size the failures are deploys, not builds: three
`deploy-pages` runs timed out at 10 minutes on 360–440 MB artifacts.

**The fix, for now: measure continuously.** `actions/site` takes `timings`
(off by default). Verbose Quartz prints a line per emitted file, so
nucleation's log would gain about 49k lines a build. The weekly run turns it
on and uploads `site-perf`: step durations, Quartz phases, the per-emitter
timeline, the slowest markdown files and output bytes by kind. The
per-emitter timeline is what will say whether social cards, the content
index or the HTML itself dominate emit, which the CI history can't.
`site_perf` was fired once on a real Quartz log and output (strata-g's
record, built locally): it read all four phases, and found 361 social cards
(7.5 MB) and 39 demo videos (99.7 MB) in 127.9 MB of output.

**LadybugDB, checked before proposing it** ([ADR-146](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-146.md)). `ladybug` 0.23.0
wrote a two-node, one-edge database to a single 96 KB file;
`@ladybugdb/wasm-core` 0.23.0 (the Node variant, loading the bytes into its
in-memory filesystem, as a browser would) opened it read-only and answered
the same Cypher query. The browser variant itself wasn't run. Its default
build needs no cross-origin isolation, which GitHub Pages can't provide; the
worker is 25.7 MB raw and 4.4 MB gzipped.
